summary: A 1977 Telnet option for remote controlled transmission and echoing, so the server can control when the user's side sends characters and echoes them. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing (RCTE) lets a serving computer direct when a user's computer shows typed text and sends it. The user's computer can collect input into groups instead of sending every character at once.

subtitle: A Telnet option for controlling terminal echo and sending input in useful groups.

tldr.problem: Echoing each typed character from a remote host can add delay, and sending every keystroke separately uses network traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The serving host sends RCTE commands that set character classes and echo behavior; the using host buffers input and follows those instructions.
tldr.outcome: The design aims to reduce echo traffic and user-to-server messages, but the RFC says its overhead is not justified for character-at-a-time use.

today: RFC 726 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Control Transmission and Echoing
sections.content:
The RFC addresses echo delay when a user connects to a full-duplex host over a satellite link. The serving host can direct the using host's terminal printer, reducing the need to send each echoed character back across the network. The using host also buffers terminal input until it forms a useful unit, reducing the number of user-to-server messages.

The option is intended for full-duplex hosts. The RFC says the Go-Ahead feature is adequate for half-duplex servers; while RCTE is active, Suppress Go-Ahead should be in force and the Echo option should not be.
sections.plainLanguage: With a distant host, waiting for every typed character to return as echo can be slow. RCTE lets the local computer show text under the host's instructions and send input in groups.

sections.title: Negotiation and RCTE Commands
sections.content:
The Telnet option is named RCTE and has code 7. The serving host offers or uses it with IAC WILL RCTE; the using host agrees or requests it with IAC DO RCTE. The serving host sends subcommands containing a command byte and, when requested, bytes that select break and transmission character classes.

A break character makes the using host send accumulated text and stop its print-or-skip action until another command arrives. A transmission character recommends sending the accumulated text. The command byte also controls whether the text before a break and the break itself are echoed. Initially, no character classes are active.
sections.plainLanguage: The two computers first agree to use RCTE. The serving computer then sends instructions that identify when to send input and whether to show the text or its ending character.

sections.title: Handling Input and Keeping the Hosts in Step
sections.content:
After negotiation, the using host prints incoming network data and processes terminal input according to the latest RCTE command. When it processes a break character, it sends the accumulated input and waits for the serving host's next break reset command before resuming the controlled printing cycle. Output from the server can also arrive spontaneously and is printed.

The serving host is expected to send one break reset command for each break character sent by the using host. If the hosts need to resynchronize, the RFC describes using Telnet Abort Output and SYNCH signals, followed by a break reset command from the serving host.
sections.plainLanguage: The local computer follows the latest instructions while it handles typed input. Each break character must be matched by a new instruction from the serving computer, and the RFC gives signals for restoring that coordination.

sections.title: Buffering and Limits
sections.content:
The transmission classes are guidelines, not mandatory limits: the using host may send a character at a time, although the RFC says that wastes RCTE. Typed-ahead input may be sent before the using host knows how to classify a character, so it may need to hold that text until a later command permits printing. If the input buffer fills and typed text will be lost, the using host should notify the user.

The RFC describes RCTE as having rather large overhead. It says this overhead is not justified in a true character-at-a-time situation, but expects average savings in network traffic and host wake-ups.
sections.plainLanguage: The user's computer may have to hold typed text while it waits for new instructions. RCTE adds its own overhead, so the RFC says it is a poor fit when every character must be sent immediately.
